analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing data-breach victims into private arbitration instead of court.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with a single sponsor and zero cosponsors, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and a subcommittee, where it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies often write "forced arbitration" clauses into customer agreements, requiring customers to settle disputes in private arbitration instead of court. This bill would ban companies from applying such clauses to disputes over a data security breach, including identity theft, and would void clauses already in existing agreements [S2][S3]. Breach victims could sue in court for damages plus attorney's fees, and the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could also enforce the ban [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose personal data is exposed in a breach. Today, if a company's customer agreement has an arbitration clause, a breach victim generally cannot join a class action or see a jury; they must take the case to a private arbitrator, alone, with no appeal. The bill would let them sue in court, recover damages, litigation costs, and attorney's fees, and reach companies' officers and employees who knowingly aided a violation [S3]. State attorneys general could also sue on residents' behalf [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits companies from requiring customers to agree, in a customer or similar agreement, to arbitrate any dispute related to a security breach, including identity theft, and voids provisions in agreements already in force that violate the ban [S2][S3].

Gives breach victims a right to sue in court for rescission, restitution, all damages, and injunctive relief, with the company paying litigation costs, reasonable attorney's fees, and expert witness fees; a two-year statute of limitations runs from discovery of the violation, and the right is cumulative with other federal and state remedies [S3].

Adds public enforcement: the Federal Trade Commission treats violations as unfair or deceptive practices and writes rules, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents, with FTC involvement and coordination provisions [S2][S3].

Extends liability to every person who controls a liable company, its partners, principal executive officers, directors, and employees who materially aid the violation, holding them jointly and severally liable unless they had no knowledge of the facts behind the violation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that hold consumers' personal data, and the individuals who run them. They would lose the protection of arbitration clauses for breach disputes and face court suits, including class actions, with damages, fee awards, and personal liability for executives and employees who knowingly aid violations [S3]. Some of that litigation cost would likely flow through to customers in prices, and the bill would shift breach disputes from a lower-cost private forum to the courts [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill stacks broad liability: every controlling person, officer, director, and even employees who 'materially aid' a violation are jointly and severally liable, which spreads breach litigation costs widely and could be passed to consumers through higher prices [S3].

A good-faith objection to any forced-arbitration ban: arbitration is often faster and cheaper for an individual claimant than court litigation, so moving breach disputes to court mainly helps cases large enough for class actions, while small individual claims may still go unfiled [S3].

The bill covers only breach-related disputes; companies could still force arbitration for every other kind of consumer dispute, so the protection is narrow relative to the full problem of forced arbitration [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and concrete: after a breach, customers with real losses could pursue them in court as a group, with fees shifting to the company that lost the data, instead of being funnelled one-by-one into private arbitration [S2][S3]. The costs are modest and mostly fall on the companies holding the data, though personal liability for officers and employees is unusually broad and the bill does nothing about forced arbitration outside the breach context [S3]. The honest limitation is that the bill never moved at all: with no cosponsors and no committee action, it was never tested, amended, or debated, so no version of it ever faced scrutiny [S4][S5].

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and a subcommittee for two years and died when the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on January 8, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5].
On January 25, 2019, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, where it remained with no further action listed for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party and never reached a committee vote or the House floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that write mandatory arbitration clauses into customer agreements, such as retailers, tech platforms, and credit bureaus, are better off: they kept the ability to route data-breach disputes into private arbitration and away from court class actions, and they never had to defend the bill on its merits because no hearing or vote ever happened [S3][S5].

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made the case for it as the sole sponsor; no other member cosponsored it

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from January 2019 onward, never scheduling a markup or reporting it out

against.name: Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce
against.role: Subcommittee of referral, House Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 25, 2019 and took no recorded action for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no positions were recorded; it had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.industry: Consumer-data companies (retailers, tech platforms, credit bureaus)
industries.note: These companies rely on arbitration clauses to keep breach victims out of court, where class actions can aggregate small losses into large awards. The bill would strip that protection for breach disputes and add executive liability, so its interest runs against the consumers it holds data for [S3].

Mandatory arbitration clauses route a stream of consumer disputes to private arbitrators for paid proceedings. By sending breach disputes back to the courts, the bill would cut off that business for one category of claims [S2][S3].

Breach victims would gain a court right with statutory attorney's fees, creating work for lawyers who file consumer class actions. The fee provision makes those cases financially viable for small individual claimants [S3].
